evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

evidence_cards.definition: Edited annual hours adults report spending on their own visits and prescriptions, on others' visits, on medical bills and insurance, and on health care paperwork; plus the share who cared for a friend or family member in the past 30 days. evidence_cards.source_locator: MEPS HC-256 (2024 Full-Year Consolidated): EQMVAM53, EQOVAM53, EQMBAM53, EQPPAM53, EQCARE53, ESAQWT24F
comparability: All U.S. adults who answered the questionnaire, not people with Lyme disease or Long COVID: MEPS cannot identify either condition reliably (AHRQ, 2026-09-24).
Fielded in 2024 only: the questionnaire was funded for that year, so there is no trend and no later update.

About 6% of respondents skipped each time item, and MEPS notes that about 20% of those who completed the paper version gave no answer to them.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire document is a biostatistical reanalysis of four NIH-funded randomized, placebo-controlled trials of antibiotic retreatment in patients with persistent symptoms following standard treatment for Lyme disease (Lyme borreliosis, caused by Borrelia burgdorferi); Long COVID is never mentioned.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed biostatistical reanalysis of the four NIH-funded randomized, placebo-controlled trials that current (as of the paper's 2012 publication) Lyme disease guidelines relied on to recommend against antibiotic retreatment for patients with persistent symptoms after a standard course of treatment. The authors argue that the two Klempner trials, and one outcome in the Krupp trial, were designed around unrealistically large target treatment effects and were likely underpowered, so their 'no significant benefit' conclusions do not prove retreatment is ineffective. The Krupp trial's fatigue outcome showed a statistically significant, sustained improvement with retreatment; the Fallon trial's 12-week cognitive-function outcome did not reach statistical significance by the paper's own threshold (p=0.053 vs. its stated p<0.05 cutoff) and was not sustained at 24 weeks, while secondary Fallon analyses found improvement in fatigue, pain, and physical functioning specifically among patients with worse baseline symptom severity. The paper reports trial-level counts of treatment-related adverse events (e.g., 6 of 55 Krupp participants; 7 of 37 Fallon participants, 18.9%) but provides no dollar costs, productivity-loss, caregiving, or insurance-access data for Lyme disease.

contextual_issues: Document states long-term persistent illness following a 30-day antibiotic course for Lyme disease is 'not uncommon, particularly when treatment is delayed,' but gives no percentage, rate, or quantified delay for this.

Document notes multiple trials found morbidity in persistently symptomatic patients 'similar to that of multiple sclerosis or congestive heart failure,' a qualitative severity comparison with no burden metric specific to this document.

Document recommends future trials investigate oral antibiotic regimens 'likely to be safer... and less costly than ceftriaxone,' implying a cost difference between IV and oral regimens without quantifying it.

Document describes ongoing medical-community debate/disagreement over whether persistent infection exists and whether retreatment helps, implying diagnostic uncertainty and fragmented care, but does not quantify care-seeking patterns, repeated visits, or patient navigation burden.

Krupp trial notes only 16% of participants were OspA-antigen positive at baseline, illustrating diagnostic/laboratory limitations, but this is a lab-marker prevalence within the trial, not a broader diagnostic-delay or access-barrier metric.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost figures (e.g., price of ceftriaxone, hospitalization, infusion administration, physician visits) are reported anywhere in the document.
No direct non-medical cost data (travel, paid help, home IV administration support) are reported.
No indirect cost data (lost income, productivity loss, caregiving time) are reported for patients or caregivers.
No insurance coverage, reimbursement, or access-barrier data for retreatment are reported.
No long-term or lifetime cost projections are given; the document's time horizons are limited to 3- and 6-month trial follow-up windows.
No demographic breakdowns (sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroup) are reported for any outcome, including adverse events.
No quantified comparison of IV ceftriaxone cost versus oral antibiotic cost is provided, despite a qualitative claim that oral regimens are 'less costly.'
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool or treat as a single 'retreatment benefit' range the results from the four trials (Klempner seropositive n=78, Klempner seronegative n=51, Krupp STOP-LD n=55, Fallon n=37): they differ in population (IgG seropositive vs. seronegative status; broad musculoskeletal/cognitive symptoms vs. severe fatigue only vs. prior-treated memory impairment only), in primary outcome definition (categorical SF-36 change vs. continuous FSS-11 fatigue scale vs. multi-domain cognitive z-score composite), and in measurement time window (3 and/or 6 months, with Fallon's subjects having already received prior IV ceftriaxone before enrollment unlike the other three trials) - these are structurally different measurements, not one quantity at different confidence levels.

Document explicitly states that combining the Klempner seropositive and seronegative trial data is 'not valid without accounting for the stratification of patients in the analysis,' which the original trial publication did not do; any simulator must not merge these two trial arms into one pooled figure.

The Krupp (6/55) and Fallon (7/37, 18.9%) adverse-event counts are small, trial-specific tallies from distinct patient populations and time windows; they should not be pooled into a single 'Lyme retreatment adverse event rate' or treated as a population-level incidence estimate.

No price year applies to any cost-related statement in this document, since no dollar figures are given; a qualitative 'less costly' comparison (IV vs. oral antibiotics) must not be assigned an invented dollar value.

systemic_gap_caveat.description: The document describes treatment guidelines for persistent Lyme symptoms as resting on four RCTs that it argues were underpowered or analyzed with statistically inefficient methods, while noting that 'until a sensitive laboratory test for active infection is clinically available,' these trials remain 'the cornerstone of treatment guideline recommendations' - i.e., clinical guidance and research direction are built on evidence the paper itself says cannot support strong conclusions.
systemic_gap_caveat.basis: Introduction ('Until a sensitive laboratory test for active infection is clinically available, clinical trials evaluating retreatment in persistently symptomatic Lyme disease patients provide the cornerstone of treatment guideline recommendations') and Discussion ('misinterpretation of insignificant findings from underpowered or poorly designed trials can have profound ramifications on treatment guideline recommendations, patient care and the direction of future research').

decision_relevance.summary: This document could inform clinicians, Lyme disease patients/advocates, and research funders or guideline panels evaluating whether antibiotic retreatment should be considered for patients with persistent symptoms after standard Lyme treatment. It contains no cost, insurance, or productivity data, so it cannot by itself answer financial what-if questions about retreatment; its value is in clarifying which trial findings about benefit and harm are statistically well-supported versus likely artifacts of underpowered study design, and in flagging where treatment guidelines may have overstated the strength of 'no benefit' conclusions. Clinicians and patients weighing retreatment could use the documented adverse-event counts and the fatigue/cognitive effect-size findings as qualitative risk-benefit inputs, while trial designers or funders could use the power/sample-size critique to scope better-designed future retreatment trials.
use_cases: A clinician or patient considering IV ceftriaxone retreatment for persistent Lyme symptoms could weigh the trial-specific adverse-event counts (Krupp: 6/55; Fallon: 7/37, 18.9%) against the Krupp fatigue-improvement finding and the Fallon secondary pain/physical-function findings in patients with worse baseline severity, understanding these are small, trial-specific counts rather than population-wide incidence or benefit rates.

A guideline panel or research funder designing future retreatment RCTs could use the document's sample-size and minimum-clinically-important-difference critique (e.g., the finding that the Klempner trials' design treatment effects were several times larger than published MCIDs) to set more realistic, adequately powered enrollment targets and avoid repeating the same design flaws.

spec.title: Lyme Antibiotic Retreatment Trials: Statistical Power and Adverse-Event Reanalysis
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces only the statistical significance findings and trial-specific adverse-event counts reported in a biostatistical reanalysis of four NIH-funded randomized, placebo-controlled Lyme disease antibiotic-retreatment trials. It contains no dollar costs, productivity-loss, caregiving-time, or insurance-access data, because the document reports none; it must not be used to answer financial what-if questions about retreatment. It also does not pool the four trials' differing populations, outcome measures, or follow-up windows into a single benefit or harm estimate, because the document explicitly states this would not be valid.

takeaway.patient: Using the document's own reported numbers, one trial (Fallon) tested whether retreatment improved cognitive function after 12 weeks; its result (a p-value of 0.053) narrowly missed the paper's own cutoff for calling a result statistically significant (meaning unlikely to be due to chance) of p<0.05, and the improvement was not sustained by 24 weeks. A separate trial (Krupp) found a statistically significant, sustained improvement in fatigue with retreatment. Both trials also reported some patients experiencing treatment-related side effects: about 11 percent of Krupp's 55 participants and about 19 percent of Fallon's 37 participants. This document has no cost or insurance information, so it cannot tell you what retreatment would cost or whether it would be covered.
takeaway.care: This reanalysis distinguishes outcome domains that are often discussed together as one 'retreatment benefit' question but had different evidence strength: the Krupp trial's fatigue outcome reached statistical significance and was sustained, while the Fallon trial's 12-week cognitive-function outcome (p=0.053 against the paper's own p<0.05 threshold) did not reach significance and was not sustained at 24 weeks, though secondary Fallon analyses found improvement in fatigue, pain, and physical functioning among patients with worse baseline severity. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in both trials (6 of 55 Krupp patients, including 3 sepsis cases in placebo and 1 anaphylaxis case in the ceftriaxone arm; 7 of 37 Fallon patients, 18.9%, mostly in the active arm).
takeaway.policy: The reanalysis argues that the Klempner trials and one Fallon outcome were designed around target treatment effects much larger than published minimum clinically important differences, making their 'no significant benefit' conclusions potentially a power/design artifact rather than proof of no effect. The paper states that until a sensitive laboratory test for active Lyme infection exists, these four trials remain the evidentiary cornerstone of treatment guidelines, even though it argues they cannot support strong conclusions. Adverse-event counts (Krupp 6/55; Fallon 7/37, 18.9%) are pooled trial totals with no demographic breakdown.

patient: If discussing retreatment with a clinician, consider raising that the fatigue-improvement finding and the cognitive-function finding came from different trials with different results, rather than treating 'retreatment works' as one single yes/no answer.

Consider asking what is known about side effects of retreatment, since both trials described here reported some patients experiencing treatment-related reactions, including a small number of serious ones.
Because this document has no cost, insurance, or coverage information, look to other sources for questions about what retreatment would cost or whether it would be covered.

Keep in mind the paper itself notes these trials differed in which patients were enrolled and how symptoms were measured, so a finding from one trial may not describe what would happen in a different situation.
care: When counseling patients about retreatment, distinguish the statistically significant, sustained fatigue finding (Krupp) from the Fallon cognitive-function finding, which missed the paper's own significance threshold and was not sustained at 24 weeks, rather than presenting 'retreatment' as one undifferentiated question.

This reanalysis's critique of trial power and effect-size assumptions may be worth considering when weighing how strictly to apply existing guideline language against retreatment for patients with severe persistent symptoms.
Given the reported adverse events (including sepsis and anaphylaxis cases), monitoring protocols for IV retreatment could be reviewed against the specific event types documented here.

Because the four trials enrolled structurally different populations (seropositive/seronegative status, fatigue-only vs. cognitive-impairment criteria, prior treatment history), avoid generalizing one trial's result to patients who more closely resemble a different trial's population.
policy: Consider whether future retreatment trials should be powered around more realistic, evidence-based effect-size targets, as the reanalysis argues the original Klempner trials were not.
This reanalysis's statistical critique may be worth weighing when reviewing whether current guideline language accurately reflects what these four trials can and cannot support.

Note that the adverse-event figures reported here are pooled trial totals without breakdown by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; disaggregated analysis using federal survey data sources such as NHIS or BRFSS could be considered for future evidence-building, though this document did not perform one.

The document frames the absence of a sensitive laboratory test for active infection as a systemic gap keeping guidelines dependent on these four trials; this could inform decisions about where to direct future research investment.

inputs.label: Fallon trial 12-week cognitive-function p-value
inputs.source: Document Results, Section 3 (Fallon trial 12-week cognitive-function outcome, p=0.053); 0.01-0.2 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the Fallon trial's actual reported p-value for its 12-week cognitive-function outcome; moving it shows how close the result was to the paper's own significance cutoff and how a slightly different value would change whether it counted as statistically significant.

inputs.label: Significance threshold (p-value cutoff)
inputs.source: Document applies p<0.05 as its own cutoff when describing the Fallon trial result; 0.01-0.1 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the conventional significance cutoff the paper itself applies; changing it shows how a different cutoff convention would change whether the same Fallon result counts as statistically significant.

inputs.label: Krupp trial treatment-related adverse events (count)
inputs.source: Document Section 3.2.1, Krupp et al. STOP-LD trial summary (6 of 55 randomized patients with significant adverse events); range reflects the trial's own enrollment size, not an assumed bound
inputs.interpretation: This is the count of Krupp trial participants with significant treatment-related adverse events, including 4 serious events (3 sepsis in placebo, 1 anaphylaxis in ceftriaxone); it is the numerator for the Krupp adverse-event rate below.

inputs.label: Krupp trial total randomized patients
inputs.source: Document Section 3.2.1 (55 total randomized: 28 ceftriaxone, 27 placebo); 10-100 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the Krupp trial's total enrolled sample size, used as the denominator for the adverse-event rate; changing it shows how the same event count would translate into a different rate in a differently sized trial.

inputs.label: Fallon trial treatment-related adverse events (count)
inputs.source: Document Section 3.3.1, Fallon et al. trial summary (7 of 37 randomized subjects, 18.9%, with significant treatment-related adverse events); range reflects the trial's own enrollment size, not an assumed bound
inputs.interpretation: This is the count of Fallon trial participants with significant treatment-related adverse events, 6 of which occurred in the active-treatment arm; it is the numerator for the Fallon adverse-event rate below.

inputs.label: Fallon trial total randomized patients
inputs.source: Document Section 3.3.1 (37 total randomized: 23 ceftriaxone, 14 placebo); 10-80 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the Fallon trial's total enrolled sample size, used as the denominator for the adverse-event rate; changing it shows how the same event count would translate into a different rate in a differently sized trial.

outputs.label: Fallon p-value minus significance threshold (positive = missed cutoff; negative = crossed cutoff)
outputs.interpretation: At the document's reported default values (p=0.053 vs. a 0.05 cutoff) this is positive by 0.003, meaning the Fallon trial's 12-week cognitive-function outcome narrowly missed statistical significance by the paper's own threshold; the paper also reports this effect was not sustained at 24 weeks. A negative value here would mean the result crossed the cutoff into significance.

outputs.label: Krupp trial adverse-event rate
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of Krupp trial participants (out of 55 randomized) who experienced a significant treatment-related adverse event, including 4 serious events; it sits alongside a trial where the targeted fatigue outcome was statistically significant and sustained, so this rate reflects a safety signal in a trial that also showed a confirmed benefit for its primary outcome.

outputs.label: Fallon trial adverse-event rate
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of Fallon trial participants (out of 37 randomized) who experienced a significant treatment-related adverse event; the document reports this trial's primary 12-week cognitive-function outcome did not reach statistical significance and was not sustained at 24 weeks, so this rate reflects a safety signal in a trial where the targeted benefit was not clearly shown, distinct from the Krupp rate above.

outputs.label: Fallon minus Krupp adverse-event rate (positive = Fallon higher; negative = Krupp higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is an illustrative side-by-side comparison of two trial-specific adverse-event rates from different patient populations, outcome measures, and follow-up windows (Fallon's subjects had already received prior IV ceftriaxone, unlike Krupp's). The document does not treat these as comparable population-level incidence rates, so this difference should not be read as a single Lyme-retreatment harm rate, only as a view of two separate trials' own reported counts side by side.

scenarios.label: Krupp: serious events only
scenarios.goal: Tests whether the Krupp adverse-event rate depends on event severity classification.
scenarios.description: Using only the 4 serious adverse events (3 sepsis, 1 anaphylaxis) instead of all 6 reported events, as the trial itself separately classifies severity, changes the computed Krupp adverse-event rate.

scenarios.label: Fallon: active arm only
scenarios.goal: Tests whether Fallon's adverse-event rate reflects mainly the active-treatment arm.
scenarios.description: Restricting the count to the ceftriaxone arm's 6 events out of its 23 patients, instead of the full 37-patient trial, shows the adverse-event rate concentrated in the active arm, as the trial itself reports this split.

scenarios.label: Krupp: active arm only
scenarios.goal: Tests whether ceftriaxone-arm patients alone show a different adverse-event rate.
scenarios.description: Using only the ceftriaxone arm's 3 events (1 anaphylaxis, 2 minor allergic reactions) out of its 28 patients, instead of the full 55-patient trial, isolates the antibiotic-arm-specific adverse-event rate, as the trial attributes each event to an arm.

scenarios.label: Krupp: placebo arm only
scenarios.goal: Tests whether placebo-arm patients alone also show meaningful adverse-event risk.
scenarios.description: Using only the placebo arm's 3 sepsis events out of its 27 patients, instead of the full 55-patient trial, shows serious events were not exclusive to the antibiotic arm, as the trial attributes each event to an arm.

scenarios.label: Stricter significance threshold
scenarios.goal: Tests whether Fallon's borderline result survives an illustrative stricter significance threshold.
scenarios.description: Lowering the significance threshold to 0.01, an illustrative stricter cutoff than the trial's own 0.05, widens the gap showing Fallon's p=0.053 result remains clearly non-significant.

scenarios.label: More lenient significance threshold
scenarios.goal: Tests whether Fallon's borderline result would pass under a more lenient threshold.
scenarios.description: Raising the significance threshold to 0.1, an illustrative more lenient cutoff than the trial's own 0.05, flips the significance gap negative, meaning Fallon's p=0.053 result would cross the cutoff.

The document reports no dollar costs, productivity-loss, caregiving, or insurance-access data, so this simulator does not model financial burden — only the significance and adverse-event findings the paper itself reports.

**Inputs.** The Fallon p-value (0.053) and the paper's own significance cutoff (p<0.05) come from the document's reported Fallon 12-week cognitive-function outcome. The Krupp adverse-event count (6 of 55 patients, including 4 serious events: 3 sepsis in the placebo arm and 1 anaphylaxis in the ceftriaxone arm) and the Fallon adverse-event count (7 of 37 patients, 18.9%, 6 of which were in the active arm) come directly from each trial's own summary section. Slider ranges beyond each observed default are assumed exploration bounds chosen for this simulator, not values the document specifies, as noted on each input.

**Outputs.** The significance-gap output shows how close the Fallon cognitive-function result came to the paper's own threshold; at the reported default it is positive, meaning the result narrowly missed significance, and the paper notes this effect was not sustained at 24 weeks. The two adverse-event-rate outputs recompute each trial's own counts as a percentage of that trial's own enrollment. The Krupp rate sits alongside a trial where the targeted fatigue outcome was statistically significant and sustained; the Fallon rate sits alongside a trial where the targeted cognitive-function outcome was not, which is why only the Fallon rate is tagged as reflecting harm in a trial that did not clearly show benefit for its target outcome. The difference between the two rates is included only as an illustrative side-by-side comparison — the document treats the four trials as structurally different (differing populations, outcome definitions, and follow-up windows, with Fallon's subjects having already received prior ceftriaxone) and explicitly does not pool them into one Lyme-retreatment harm rate.

**Limitations.** The adverse-event counts here are pooled trial-level totals with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status; federal survey data sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support disaggregated analysis of this kind even though this document did not perform one. Separately, the document describes a systemic evidence gap: until a sensitive laboratory test for active Lyme infection becomes available, it states these four trials — which it argues were underpowered or statistically inefficient — remain the cornerstone of treatment guideline recommendations, meaning clinical guidance rests on evidence the paper itself says cannot support strong conclusions. This document does not address Long COVID and provides no basis for cost-effectiveness or economic-burden estimates.

spec.title: Lyme Antibiotic Retreatment Trials: Statistical Power and Adverse-Event Reanalysis
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces only the statistical significance findings and trial-specific adverse-event counts reported in a biostatistical reanalysis of four NIH-funded randomized, placebo-controlled Lyme disease antibiotic-retreatment trials. It contains no dollar costs, productivity-loss, caregiving-time, or insurance-access data, because the document reports none; it must not be used to answer financial what-if questions about retreatment. It also does not pool the four trials' differing populations, outcome measures, or follow-up windows into a single benefit or harm estimate, because the document explicitly states this would not be valid.

takeaway.patient: Using the document's own reported numbers, one trial (Fallon) tested whether retreatment improved cognitive function after 12 weeks; its result (a p-value of 0.053) narrowly missed the paper's own cutoff for calling a result statistically significant (meaning unlikely to be due to chance) of p<0.05, and the improvement was not sustained by 24 weeks. A separate trial (Krupp) found a statistically significant, sustained improvement in fatigue with retreatment. Both trials also reported some patients experiencing treatment-related side effects: about 11 percent of Krupp's 55 participants and about 19 percent of Fallon's 37 participants. This document has no cost or insurance information, so it cannot tell you what retreatment would cost or whether it would be covered.
takeaway.care: This reanalysis distinguishes outcome domains that are often discussed together as one 'retreatment benefit' question but had different evidence strength: the Krupp trial's fatigue outcome reached statistical significance and was sustained, while the Fallon trial's 12-week cognitive-function outcome (p=0.053 against the paper's own p<0.05 threshold) did not reach significance and was not sustained at 24 weeks, though secondary Fallon analyses found improvement in fatigue, pain, and physical functioning among patients with worse baseline severity. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in both trials (6 of 55 Krupp patients, including 3 sepsis cases in placebo and 1 anaphylaxis case in the ceftriaxone arm; 7 of 37 Fallon patients, 18.9%, mostly in the active arm).
takeaway.policy: The reanalysis argues that the Klempner trials and one Fallon outcome were designed around target treatment effects much larger than published minimum clinically important differences, making their 'no significant benefit' conclusions potentially a power/design artifact rather than proof of no effect. The paper states that until a sensitive laboratory test for active Lyme infection exists, these four trials remain the evidentiary cornerstone of treatment guidelines, even though it argues they cannot support strong conclusions. Adverse-event counts (Krupp 6/55; Fallon 7/37, 18.9%) are pooled trial totals with no demographic breakdown.

patient: If discussing retreatment with a clinician, consider raising that the fatigue-improvement finding and the cognitive-function finding came from different trials with different results, rather than treating 'retreatment works' as one single yes/no answer.

Consider asking what is known about side effects of retreatment, since both trials described here reported some patients experiencing treatment-related reactions, including a small number of serious ones.
Because this document has no cost, insurance, or coverage information, look to other sources for questions about what retreatment would cost or whether it would be covered.

Keep in mind the paper itself notes these trials differed in which patients were enrolled and how symptoms were measured, so a finding from one trial may not describe what would happen in a different situation.
care: When counseling patients about retreatment, distinguish the statistically significant, sustained fatigue finding (Krupp) from the Fallon cognitive-function finding, which missed the paper's own significance threshold and was not sustained at 24 weeks, rather than presenting 'retreatment' as one undifferentiated question.

This reanalysis's critique of trial power and effect-size assumptions may be worth considering when weighing how strictly to apply existing guideline language against retreatment for patients with severe persistent symptoms.
Given the reported adverse events (including sepsis and anaphylaxis cases), monitoring protocols for IV retreatment could be reviewed against the specific event types documented here.

Because the four trials enrolled structurally different populations (seropositive/seronegative status, fatigue-only vs. cognitive-impairment criteria, prior treatment history), avoid generalizing one trial's result to patients who more closely resemble a different trial's population.
policy: Consider whether future retreatment trials should be powered around more realistic, evidence-based effect-size targets, as the reanalysis argues the original Klempner trials were not.
This reanalysis's statistical critique may be worth weighing when reviewing whether current guideline language accurately reflects what these four trials can and cannot support.

Note that the adverse-event figures reported here are pooled trial totals without breakdown by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; disaggregated analysis using federal survey data sources such as NHIS or BRFSS could be considered for future evidence-building, though this document did not perform one.

The document frames the absence of a sensitive laboratory test for active infection as a systemic gap keeping guidelines dependent on these four trials; this could inform decisions about where to direct future research investment.

outputs.label: Fallon p-value minus significance threshold (positive = missed cutoff; negative = crossed cutoff)
outputs.interpretation: At the document's reported default values (p=0.053 vs. a 0.05 cutoff) this is positive by 0.003, meaning the Fallon trial's 12-week cognitive-function outcome narrowly missed statistical significance by the paper's own threshold; the paper also reports this effect was not sustained at 24 weeks. A negative value here would mean the result crossed the cutoff into significance.

outputs.label: Krupp trial adverse-event rate
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of Krupp trial participants (out of 55 randomized) who experienced a significant treatment-related adverse event, including 4 serious events; it sits alongside a trial where the targeted fatigue outcome was statistically significant and sustained, so this rate reflects a safety signal in a trial that also showed a confirmed benefit for its primary outcome.

outputs.label: Fallon trial adverse-event rate
outputs.interpretation: This is the share of Fallon trial participants (out of 37 randomized) who experienced a significant treatment-related adverse event; the document reports this trial's primary 12-week cognitive-function outcome did not reach statistical significance and was not sustained at 24 weeks, so this rate reflects a safety signal in a trial where the targeted benefit was not clearly shown, distinct from the Krupp rate above.

outputs.label: Fallon minus Krupp adverse-event rate (positive = Fallon higher; negative = Krupp higher)
outputs.interpretation: This is an illustrative side-by-side comparison of two trial-specific adverse-event rates from different patient populations, outcome measures, and follow-up windows (Fallon's subjects had already received prior IV ceftriaxone, unlike Krupp's). The document does not treat these as comparable population-level incidence rates, so this difference should not be read as a single Lyme-retreatment harm rate, only as a view of two separate trials' own reported counts side by side.

scenarios.description: Using only the placebo arm's 3 sepsis events out of its 27 patients, instead of the full 55-patient trial, shows serious events were not exclusive to the antibiotic arm, as the trial attributes each event to an arm.
